sections.markdown:
## When to recognize this pattern
Look for hierarchical nodes connected by edges, repeated work, or a prompt whose constraints rule out a quadratic scan.

## Core idea
A tree has a root and parent-child edges; a leaf has no children. A binary tree allows at most two children. A BST adds an ordering invariant. Pre-order visits node-left-right, in-order left-node-right, and post-order left-right-node. Height drives recursion depth and balance affects BST performance.

```text
        4  <- root
      /   \
     2     7
    / \     \
   1   3     9 <- leaf
```

## Naive approach
Start with repeated subtree rescans. It may be easy to verify, but it repeats work and becomes too slow as input grows. State its cost before optimizing.

## Better approach
Use recursive and iterative traversal. The optimization is valid only if the invariant proves discarded work cannot affect the answer. Never quote a complexity without identifying the operation that dominates it.

## Time complexity
O(n) traversal time. Explain whether sorting or preprocessing is included.

## Space complexity
O(h) recursion space for height h. Input storage does not count as auxiliary space unless copied.

## Common mistakes
Using the pattern without its precondition, moving state in the wrong order, missing empty input, mishandling duplicates, and reporting average-case cost as a guarantee. For recursion, include call-stack space; for a DP table or hash map, count stored states.
